title: Kirby Problem 3.2
exact_target: Prove that some hyperbolic three-manifold volumes have irrational ratios; more strongly, show that their rational span has arbitrarily large dimension.
definition_tex:
\subsection{Definitions and mathematical statement}
Let $\mathcal V$ be the set of volumes of all connected complete finite-volume
hyperbolic three-manifolds, with sectional curvature normalized to $-1$.
Volumes are positive real numbers, and a finite covering of degree $d$
multiplies volume by $d$. In particular, manifolds sharing a finite-sheeted
cover have rationally related volumes. The problem asks for rational
independence beyond this necessary relation.

The phrase ``not all rationally related'' has two versions explicitly
distinguished in the source. The first asks for manifolds $M,N$ with
\[
 \frac{\operatorname{vol}(M)}{\operatorname{vol}(N)}\notin\mathbb Q.
\]
The stronger version asks whether the vector space
$\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}\mathcal V$ is infinite-dimensional.
Equivalently, for every positive integer $r$ there should be manifolds
$M_1,\ldots,M_r$ such that
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^r q_j\operatorname{vol}(M_j)=0,
 \quad q_j\in\mathbb Q
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad q_1=\cdots=q_r=0.
\]
These assertions are recorded separately; an irrational ratio only proves
that the dimension is at least two. Likewise, proving that one volume is
irrational does not alone prove that its ratio with a second volume is irrational.

\subsection{Short English statement}
Prove that some hyperbolic three-manifold volumes have irrational ratios; more strongly, show that their rational span has arbitrarily large dimension.
